## Statement

Let $X$ be a $C^2$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, where $C^2$ means that total derivatives through order two exist and are continuous. Its local flow $\phi_X^t(q)$ from [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,q)$, and $J(t,q):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)$ satisfies $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(q))J$ and $J(0,q)=I$. For two such fields define their bracket by $[X,Y](q):=DY(q)X(q)-DX(q)Y(q)$. If $[X,Y]=0$ on a neighborhood and all local maps stay there, then $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and their local flows commute: $\phi_X^t\circ\phi_Y^s=\phi_Y^s\circ\phi_X^t$ whenever both sides are defined.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated Euclidean domains and $C^2$ regularity; for $m\ge1$ use the local contraction flow of [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]], and for $m=0$ construct the flow directly in step 1.1.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]]: for $m\ge1$, a continuous-derivative vector field has a unique local flow, a Volterra integral equation, locally Lipschitz dependence on initial data, and the local flow law.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable maps, $D(g\circ f)=Dg\circ Df$ at the corresponding point.

[F3] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] and [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: continuous coefficient functions are integrable on compact intervals, and an integrable interior derivative evaluates by its endpoint increment.

[F4] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] and [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]: a closed bounded Euclidean ball is compact, and continuous finite-dimensional derivative fields on it are uniformly continuous.

[F5] [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]]: every Euclidean Cauchy sequence in a finite-dimensional real coordinate space converges. Consequently, continuous curves into the finite-dimensional matrix and bilinear-map spaces below are complete in the supremum operator norm: a supremum-Cauchy sequence is coordinatewise uniformly Cauchy, its coordinate limits are continuous by uniform convergence, and the bounds $\|A\|_{\rm op}\le\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|$ and $\|B\|_{\rm op}\le\sum_{k,i,j}|B_{kij}|$ turn coordinatewise uniform convergence into uniform operator-norm convergence.

[F6] [[thm-banach-fixed-point]]: a contraction from a nonempty complete metric space to itself has a unique fixed point.

[F7] [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]: if all first partial derivatives of a map exist on a neighborhood and are continuous at a point, the map is totally differentiable there with the Jacobian as derivative.

## Proof

**Given:** In the case $m\ge1$, choose a compact closed ball $K$ inside the field domain and a time interval $[-\delta,\delta]$ so all flow points and line segments used below remain in $K$. By [F4], $K$ is compact; continuity of $DX$ and $D^2X$ makes $L:=\sup_K\|DX\|$ and $M_2:=\sup_K\|D^2X\|$ finite. Shrink $\delta$ so $L\delta<1$. Write $M_m(\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for real matrices acting as linear maps on $\mathbb R^m$, and write $\operatorname{Bil}(\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R^m)$ for bilinear maps. Matrix and bilinear-map norms are operator norms induced by the Euclidean norm; vector-valued integrals are componentwise Riemann integrals.

1.1 For $m=0$, define $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton consisting of the empty coordinate tuple, denoted $0$, with its unique vector-space structure and norm $\|0\|=0$. Its open subsets are empty or the singleton; the empty domain has no initial point and all assertions there are vacuous. On the singleton both fields necessarily equal zero. Define $\phi_X^t(0)=\phi_Y^t(0)=0$ for every real $t$. These are the unique solution curves and satisfy the flow law. Every map into this zero vector space has the unique zero linear map as total derivative, since its differentiability remainder is identically zero; iterating gives continuous derivatives through order two. Thus the flows are jointly $C^2$, $J$ is the unique endomorphism of $\mathbb R^0$, which is also its identity $I_0$, and $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X)J=0$. The bracket and both transport expressions are zero, and both flow compositions are the identity. This proves every assertion for $m=0$ without invoking the positive-dimensional suppliers. In the remaining steps assume $m\ge1$. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For $p$ near $q$ put $\Delta_h(t):=\phi_X^t(p+h)-\phi_X^t(p)$. The integral equations from [F1] and the one-variable fundamental theorem applied to $\theta\mapsto X(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))$ give $$\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_0^t A_h(s)\Delta_h(s)\,ds,\quad A_h(s):=\int_0^1DX(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))\,d\theta.$$ The segments lie in $K$ after shrinking the initial ball and time interval. The local Lipschitz estimate in [F1] gives $\sup_t\|\Delta_h(t)\|=O(\|h\|)$. Uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$ from [F4] makes $A_h(s)$ converge uniformly to $DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ as $h\to0$. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 Let $\mathcal I=[-\delta,\delta]$ and let $\mathcal C_1=C(\mathcal I,M_m(\mathbb R))$ with the supremum operator norm. This space is complete: for a supremum-Cauchy sequence $(J_k)$, each matrix entry at each $s$ is Cauchy because $|A_{ij}|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$; [F5] applied to the $m^2$ entries gives a pointwise matrix limit $J(s)$, and the uniform Cauchy estimate passed to each entry gives uniform convergence of all entries. Each limit entry is continuous by the $\varepsilon/3$ argument for uniform limits of continuous functions. The finite-coordinate bound $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|$ then gives uniform operator-norm convergence, so $J\in\mathcal C_1$. The space is nonempty because it contains the constant zero matrix curve. Put $A_0(s):=DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ and define $T(J)(t):=I_m+\int_0^t A_0(s)J(s)\,ds$. It maps $\mathcal C_1$ into itself and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta<1$. By [F6], it has a unique fixed point $J$. Define $R_h(t):=\Delta_h(t)-J(t)h$. Subtracting the integral equations and writing the integrand difference as $(A_h-A_0)\Delta_h+A_0R_h$ gives $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+\delta\|A_h-A_0\|_\infty\|\Delta_h\|_\infty=o(\|h\|)$, by step 1.2 and uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$. Thus $D_q\phi_X^t(p)=J(t,p)$. The continuous integrand in the equation for $J$ has average over $[t,t+h]$ tending to its value at $t$: the quotient error is at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|DX(\phi_X^s(p))J(s,p)-DX(\phi_X^t(p))J(t,p)\|$, which tends to zero. Thus $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(p))J$ and $J(0,p)=I_m$. [step 1.2, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

3.1 Write $J_h(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p+h)$ and $J_0(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p)$. Subtracting their integral equations gives $J_h-J_0=\int_0^t A_0(J_h-J_0)\,ds+\int_0^t(A_h-A_0)J_h\,ds$, where $A_h=DX(\phi_h)$, $A_0=DX(\phi_0)$, $\phi_h=\phi_X^s(p+h)$, and $\phi_0=\phi_X^s(p)$. The line-segment chain rule and Newton–Leibniz supplier claims in [F2]–[F3], applied entrywise to $DX$ along the segment from $\phi_0$ to $\phi_h$, give the exact formula $A_h-A_0=\int_0^1D^2X(\phi_0+\theta(\phi_h-\phi_0))[\phi_h-\phi_0,\cdot]\,d\theta$ and therefore $\|A_h-A_0\|_\infty\le M_2\|\phi_h-\phi_0\|_\infty$. By [F1], $\|\phi_h-\phi_0\|_\infty=O(\|h\|)$; the integral equation gives $\|J_h\|_\infty\le(1-L\delta)^{-1}$. Absorbing the first integral using $L\delta<1$ yields $J_h-J_0=O(\|h\|)$ uniformly in time. Uniform continuity of $D^2X$ on $K$, the same line-segment formula, and $\phi_h-\phi_0=J_0h+o(\|h\|)$ from step 2.1 now give $A_h-A_0=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|)$ uniformly, and hence $(A_h-A_0)J_h=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,J_0(\cdot)]+o(\|h\|)$. For each base point $p$, define $\mathcal C_2=C(\mathcal I,\operatorname{Bil}(\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R^m))$ with the supremum bilinear-operator norm. The coordinatewise completeness proof of step 2.1 applies with $m^3$ coefficients, so $\mathcal C_2$ is complete; it is nonempty because it contains the zero bilinear-map curve. The map $(\mathcal T K)(t)[u,v]:=\int_0^t\big(A_0(s)K(s)[u,v]+D^2X(\phi_0(s))[J_0(s)u,J_0(s)v]\big)\,ds$ is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$ on $\mathcal C_2$. By [F6] it has a unique fixed point $K_p$. Subtracting its equation evaluated at $(h,v)$ from the equation for $J_h-J_0$ gives $R_h:=J_h-J_0-K_p[h,\cdot]$ with $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+o(\|h\|)$, so $R_h=o(\|h\|)$. Therefore $D_pJ[h](v)=K_p[h,v]$, and $K_p$ is the second derivative $D_q^2\phi_X$. Its equation makes it bilinear. The coefficients, forcing, $\phi_p$, and $J_p$ vary continuously in $p$ uniformly for $s\in\mathcal I$; for fixed-point maps $T_p$ with contraction constant $L\delta$, $\|K_p-K_{p'}\|_\infty\le(1-L\delta)^{-1}\|T_p(K_{p'})-T_{p'}(K_{p'})\|_\infty\to0$. The integral equation gives continuity in $t$ as well. Thus the second derivatives in $q$ are continuous. [step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

3.2 Let $V(t):=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and $W(t):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)$. By [F2] and the variational equation, $V'=DY(\phi_X^t)X(\phi_X^t)$ and $W'=DX(\phi_X^t)W$. The identity $[X,Y]=0$ makes $V$ solve this same linear equation with $V(0)=W(0)=Y(q)$; uniqueness from the contraction argument gives $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$. [F1, F2, step 2.1]

4.1 On the open interior of the chosen time and initial-point neighborhood, step 2.1 gives $D_q\phi_X=J$ and $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X)J$, while step 3.1 gives the continuous second derivative $D_qJ=K$. The chain rule [F2] applied to $\partial_t\phi_X=X(\phi_X)$ gives $\partial_{q_i}\partial_t\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)Je_i$, and the variational equation gives $\partial_t\partial_{q_i}\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)Je_i$; also $\partial_t^2\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)X(\phi_X)$. Hence all first- and second-order coordinate partial derivatives of $\phi_X$ exist and are continuous there. Apply [F7] pointwise first to $\phi_X$ and then to its first-derivative map: its Jacobian is the matrix of first partials, and the Jacobian of that map is the continuous array of second partials. Thus $\phi_X$ is jointly $C^2$. [F2, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 For fixed $t$, the curve $s\mapsto\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q))$ has derivative $D\phi_X^t\,Y(\phi_Y^s(q))=Y(\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q)))$ by step 3.2, and starts at $\phi_X^t(q)$. It is therefore the $Y$-flow from that initial point; IVP uniqueness from [F1] yields $\phi_X^t\phi_Y^s(q)=\phi_Y^s\phi_X^t(q)$. [step 3.2, F1, F2] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge1$, be open, and let $\omega$ be a nowhere-zero $C^2$ one-form, with the horizontal paths of [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]. Assume that every point has a neighborhood $W$ with $S\in C^2(W)$ and nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ satisfying $dS=\mu\omega$. For every $q\in U$, its horizontal reachability class in $U$ is contained in a countable union of compact subsets of $U$ with empty interior. Consequently every nonempty open $V\subseteq U$ contains a point not horizontally reachable from $q$ by any horizontal path in $U$. In particular, if $q\in V$, that point is not reachable by a path contained in $V$. No global first integral or choice axiom is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open Euclidean domain, nowhere-zero $C^2$ form, two-sided finite-piece horizontal paths, and local first integrals in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]: a horizontal path is piecewise $C^1$, with finitely many pieces, and its tangent lies in $\ker\omega$; constant paths, reversal and finite concatenation are admissible.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] and [[lem-tdmath-variational-flow-and-commutation]]: $C^2$ vector fields have unique local $C^2$ flows, available for both time signs, with inverse flow and differentiable dependence.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: composition derivatives obey the chain rule, and a real differentiable function with zero derivative on an interval is constant.

[L1] [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]]: a $C^1$ zero equation with a specified invertible solved-coordinate minor has a local $C^1$ graph. The batch-4 draft carrier and its proof have been inspected; deductions using it remain conditional on that supplier's final acceptance.

[F4] [[thm-connected-subsets-of-r-are-intervals]]: every interval is connected; it cannot be partitioned into two nonempty relatively open sets.

[F5] [[thm-rationals-countable]] and [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]: the rational reals admit an enumeration and are dense, without a choice hypothesis. Fix an enumeration $(r_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ of them. Encode each length-$m$ flow word by its finite string in the finite alphabet of fields, and each rational closed box in $\mathbb R^m$ by the $2m$ indices of its endpoints in $(r_k)$. For each $N$, only finitely many word-box codes have $m$ plus the sum of those indices at most $N$; ordering these finite levels and then lexicographically enumerates all pairs. The same coding by dimension, center-coordinate indices, and radius index enumerates rational balls in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Coordinatewise density and a sufficiently small positive rational radius give such a ball whose closed ball lies in any prescribed nonempty open set.

[F6] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]] and [[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]: a closed bounded parameter box is compact; its continuous image is compact and closed in the Euclidean ambient space. These suppliers are choice-free.

[F7] [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]]: every Euclidean Cauchy sequence converges, coordinatewise from real completeness.

[F8] [[thm-recursion]] and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]]: a recursively prescribed least natural-number index defines a sequence without arbitrary selections.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Use the local first integrals in the Statement. Write $\omega=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\omega_j dx_j$ in the fixed Euclidean coordinates and set $w=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{n+1})$ and $Z_j=e_j-(\omega_j/|w|^2)w$. These globally defined $C^2$ vector fields are horizontal and span $\ker\omega$ at each point, since their matrix is the orthogonal projection onto that kernel. On every neighborhood supplied by the hypothesis, $dS=\mu\omega$ has nonzero derivative, and each $Z_j$-flow preserves $S$ as long as its trajectory remains there, by [F3]. Its derivative therefore preserves horizontal tangent vectors there: differentiating $S(\phi_j^t(x))=S(x)$ gives $dS_{\phi_j^t(x)}D\phi_j^t(x)v=dS_xv=0$ for horizontal $v$. The compact image of any finite flow trajectory has a finite subcover by such neighborhoods; a sufficiently fine finite subdivision of its compact time interval puts each subtrajectory in one of them. This follows directly from compactness: otherwise shrinking subintervals failing the subdivision would have a limiting time whose neighborhood contains them. Composing the local derivative identities obtains preservation over the full duration. Local flow uniqueness makes these continuations consistent, and [F2] gives $C^2$ dependence on durations and initial points wherever the finite composition is defined. [F1, F2, F3, F6, given, construct]

2.1 Fix $q\in U$ and a neighborhood $W$ with $dS=\mu\omega$ as in the hypothesis. Since $dS_q=\mu(q)\omega_q\ne0$, apply [L1] to $x\mapsto S(x)-S(q)$ with ambient dimension $n+1$ and target dimension $1$; after choosing the solved coordinate, its zero set is a local $C^1$ graph plaque $P$ through $q$, parameterized by its $n$ free coordinates. Let $\pi$ be projection to those free coordinates. Choose $n$ of the fields $Z_j$ that form a basis of $\ker\omega_q=\ker dS_q$, and for $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)$ near $0$ let $E(s)$ be the endpoint at $q$ of the successive local flows of these fields for durations $s_1,\ldots,s_n$. Shrink the open duration domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ so all flow segments stay in $W$. Step 1.1 shows that each flow preserves $S$, so $E(D)\subseteq P$; moreover $DE(0)$ has the chosen basis as its columns. The differential $D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is therefore an invertible $n\times n$ matrix, because $D\pi_q$ is an isomorphism from the tangent space of the graph plaque to its free-coordinate space. Choose an open neighborhood $Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $y_0=\pi(q)$ and shrink $D$ so that the target-augmented map $H:D\times Y\to\mathbb R^n$, $H(s,y):=\pi(E(s))-y$, is defined. It satisfies $H(0,y_0)=0$ and its solved block $D_sH(0,y_0)=D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is invertible. Apply [L1] with ambient dimension $2n$ and target dimension $n<2n$, permuting inputs to $(y,s)$ so $y$ is free and $s$ is solved. For every $y$ near $y_0$ this gives $s(y)$ with $\pi(E(s(y)))=y$; uniqueness of the graph plaque then says the endpoints $E(s(y))$ fill a relative neighborhood of $q$ in $P$. Each is reachable by a finite word of horizontal flows inside $W$. Conversely, a horizontal path preserves the local $S$ on each short subarc in a first-integral neighborhood by [F3]. Thus near each parameter value its image lies in the relative plaque neighborhood just shown to be reachable by such a finite word. The finite-word orbits are equivalence classes by flow reversal and concatenation, so their preimages along the path are relatively open in its interval domain. By [F4], connectedness of that interval forces one class. Hence every point horizontally reachable from $q$ lies in its finite-word orbit; the reverse inclusion follows because every word is a horizontal concatenation. [F1, F2, F3, F4, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For a fixed finite word $\alpha$ of length $m\ge1$, write $F_\alpha:O_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to U$ for its endpoint map from $q$, on the open set of admissible duration tuples. Each duration derivative is a field vector transported by the later flows and is horizontal by step 1.1. Near any $s\in O_\alpha$, continuity puts the endpoint image in a neighborhood with the first integral $S$ from the hypothesis; hence $D(S\circ F_\alpha)=0$. On a small convex parameter ball, [F3] makes $S\circ F_\alpha$ constant. Coordinatewise density in [F5] supplies a closed box with rational endpoints containing $s$ in its interior and contained in that ball. Its image under $F_\alpha$ is compact by [F6], lies in one level of $S$, and has empty interior in $U$: a nonempty open subset of that image would make $S$ constant on an open set, contradicting $dS=\mu\omega\ne0$. Thus the image is a closed nowhere-dense subset of $U$. Enumerate the finite-word/rational-box pairs by the finite-level coding in [F5]; for an admissible box whose compact image has empty interior record that image, and otherwise record the empty set. Include the singleton $\{q\}$ for the empty word. This sequence $(K_j)$ of closed nowhere-dense sets covers $\mathcal O(q)$, since every duration tuple admits the small box just constructed. No countable atlas or choice of first integrals is needed for the enumeration. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Let $V$ be any nonempty open subset of $U$. By [F5], choose an initial rational open ball $B_{-1}$ with $\overline{B_{-1}}\subset V$. Recursively, for each $j\ge0$, choose the first rational ball $B_j=B(c_j,r_j)$ in the fixed enumeration such that $\overline{B_j}\subset B_{j-1}\setminus K_j$ and $0<r_j<2^{-j}$. Such a ball exists: $K_j$ is closed with empty interior, so $B_{j-1}\setminus K_j$ is a nonempty open set, which contains a rational ball with closed ball inside it and arbitrarily small radius by [F5]. For $k>j$, the later centers lie in $B_j$, so $|c_k-c_j|<r_j<2^{-j}$; hence $(c_j)$ is Cauchy. By [F7] it has a limit $p$, and each tail of the sequence lies in the closed ball $\overline{B_j}$, so $p\in\overline{B_j}$ for every $j$. These closed balls lie in $V$ and satisfy $\overline{B_j}\cap K_j=\varnothing$, so $p\in V\setminus\bigcup_jK_j$. Each selection is the least natural-number index satisfying explicit conditions, so it uses no choice axiom. Since the $K_j$ cover $\mathcal O(q)$, step 2.1 shows $p$ is not horizontally reachable from $q$ even by a path in $U$, and therefore not by one in $V$. This proves the asserted conclusion for every nonempty open $V$, using no global first integral or choice axiom. [given, F5, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $v_a,v_b\in\mathbb R$ with $v_a<v_b$. A fraction $\lambda\in[0,1]$ satisfies $v=(1-\lambda)v_a+\lambda v_b$ exactly when $v\in[v_a,v_b]$ and

$$\lambda=\frac{v-v_a}{v_b-v_a}.$$

This fraction is unique. At $v=v_a$ it is $0$, and at $v=v_b$ it is $1$; no admissible fraction gives a value outside the endpoint interval.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Ordered real numbers $v_a<v_b$, an interval point $v\in\mathbb R$, and a mixing fraction $\lambda\in[0,1]$.

[F1] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: $\mathbb R$ is an ordered field, so division by the positive number $v_b-v_a$ is valid and preserves inequalities.

[F2] [[def-interval]]: $[0,1]=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:0\le\lambda\le1\}$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 From $v=(1-\lambda)v_a+\lambda v_b$ one obtains $v-v_a=\lambda(v_b-v_a)$. Since $v_b-v_a>0$ and $0\le\lambda\le1$, this gives $v_a\le v\le v_b$ and forces $\lambda=(v-v_a)/(v_b-v_a)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

The scaling is an exact identity for the displayed equations.
